samasa.sense: Śiva, whose bow is called Pināka; -धृक् ‘holding’ is an agent noun used at the end of compounds

morph.note: Past active participle (क्तवतु) of √दा, used as a finite past verb: ‘(he) gave’. The text alternates it with the perfect ददौ through the list of gifts.
Absolutive of the causative of सम् + उद् + √पद्, ‘having caused to arise’: each god produces a copy of his own weapon from it and gives the copy.
Nominative singular of a consonant-stem agent noun (-धृक्), the same in pause; see Uncertain for its derivation.

mantras.anvaya: पिनाकधृक् शूलात् शूलं विनिष्कृष्य तस्यै ददौ। कृष्णः च स्वचक्रतः चक्रं समुत्पाद्य (तस्यै) दत्तवान्।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two parallel sentences: giver, an absolutive phrase (how the weapon was made), the gift, and the verb.
mantras.lit: Drawing out a trident from (his own) trident, the bearer of Pināka gave it to her; and Kṛṣṇa, producing a discus from his own discus, gave it.
mantras.tr: Śiva, bearer of the Pināka bow, drew a trident out of his own trident and gave it to her; and Viṣṇu brought forth a discus from his own discus and gave it to her.
mantras.tr_note: tr names the givers Śiva and Viṣṇu for पिनाकधृक् and कृष्ण, and repeats ‘to her’.

comm.t: The gifts begin. Each weapon is drawn out of the god’s own weapon: the gods do not give theirs away but make a second one from it. Śiva gives the trident and Viṣṇu the discus.

The dhyāna of the middle carita in the Gita Press pāṭha (recited before 2.1) pictures Mahālakṣmī holding these gifts: trident, discus (सुदर्शन), conch, spear, bow, thunderbolt, bell, staff, noose, rosary, water-pot, sword and shield among them. The chapter supplies the story behind that iconography.

flags.uncertain: Kṛṣṇa here is a name of Viṣṇu (the discus-bearer of 2.10), not specifically the avatāra. पिनाकधृक्: the final member -धृक् ‘holding’ is common at the end of compounds; its derivation (from √धृ, or by analogy with forms of √धृष्) is not certain. GRETIL’s Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa carries additional verse material at this point (recension note in corrections.json); the Gita Press text is followed.

samasa.literal: he whose food is the oblation
samasa.sense: Agni, the fire that consumes what is offered
samasa.alt: Also analysed as an upapada-type tatpuruṣa, हुतम् अश्नाति इति ‘he who eats the oblation’ (अशन as an agent noun); the sense is the same.

morph.note: Accusative dual of इषुधि ‘quiver’ (‘that in which arrows are placed’). The noun is masculine or feminine; the feminine adjective बाणपूर्णे shows it is feminine here. Two quivers, one for each side.
Feminine accusative dual of the a-stem adjective (-ā stem in the feminine, dual -ए), agreeing with इषुधी.

mantras.anvaya: वरुणः च शङ्खं (तस्यै ददौ), हुताशनः तस्यै शक्तिं ददौ। मारुतः चापं तथा बाणपूर्णे इषुधी दत्तवान्।
mantras.anvaya_en: Three gifts: ददौ is stated once for Varuṇa’s and Agni’s gifts; Māruta’s bow and quivers take दत्तवान्.
mantras.lit: And Varuṇa (gave) a conch; Hutāśana gave her a spear; Māruta gave a bow and also two quivers full of arrows.
mantras.tr: Varuṇa gave her a conch, and Fire a spear; the Wind gave her a bow and two quivers full of arrows.

comm.t: Three more gifts: the conch from Varuṇa, lord of the waters (the conch is a sea creature), the spear (śakti) from Agni, and from the Wind a bow and two full quivers.
A modern reading: each gift fits its giver. The sea gives the conch, fire the spear, and the swift wind the bow and arrows that fly through it.

sandhi.note: Final m before a vowel stays m and is written together with the next word.
Final t is voiced to d before a vowel; likewise ऐरावताद् गजात् before the voiced g. Inside the compound, अमर + अधिप → अमराधिप (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः, 6.1.101).

samasa.sense: Indra, king of the gods (the title Mahiṣa had usurped, 2.3)

samasa.literal: he who has a thousand eyes
samasa.sense: Indra; अक्षि becomes अक्ष at the end of a bahuvrīhi (a samāsānta affix)

morph.note: As in 2.20: absolutive of the causative of सम् + उद् + √पद्. Indra makes a vajra from his own kuliśa (both words mean ‘thunderbolt’).
Ablative of source: the bell is taken from Airāvata, the elephant, who wore it. ऐरावतात् and गजात् stand in apposition.

mantras.anvaya: अमराधिपः सहस्राक्षः इन्द्रः कुलिशात् वज्रं समुत्पाद्य तस्यै ददौ, ऐरावतात् गजात् घण्टां (च ददौ)।
mantras.anvaya_en: One subject with two epithets, an absolutive phrase, the verb ददौ, and a second object (घण्टाम्) with its source.
mantras.lit: Indra, lord of the immortals, producing a thunderbolt from (his own) thunderbolt, gave it to her, the thousand-eyed one, and a bell from the elephant Airāvata.
mantras.tr: Indra, the thousand-eyed lord of the gods, brought forth a thunderbolt from his own and gave it to her, together with a bell from his elephant Airāvata.

comm.t: Indra gives a thunderbolt made from his own and the bell of his elephant Airāvata. The god whose throne Mahiṣa took is named by his full titles: lord of the immortals, the thousand-eyed.
The bell will be used in the battle: its sound stupefies the asuras (2.56, घण्टास्वनविमोहितान्), and the gods later pray that it protect them (11.27).

samasa.literal: from the staff of Kāla (Time, Death)
samasa.sense: from Yama’s own staff of death
samasa.alt: Also a karmadhāraya, कालः एव दण्डः ‘the staff that is death’; either way it is Yama’s own weapon.

morph.note: Nominative singular of the masculine n-stem ब्रह्मन् (the god Brahmā), as distinct from the neuter ब्रह्म (the Absolute).
Accusative of the u-stem कमण्डलु, the ascetic’s water-pot, Brahmā’s emblem.

mantras.anvaya: यमः कालदण्डात् दण्डं (तस्यै ददौ), अम्बुपतिः च पाशं ददौ। प्रजापतिः च अक्षमालां ददौ, ब्रह्मा कमण्डलुं (ददौ)।
mantras.anvaya_en: Four gifts in two lines; ददौ is stated twice and understood with the other two givers.
mantras.lit: Yama (gave) a staff from (his) staff of death, and the lord of the waters gave a noose; and Prajāpati gave a rosary; Brahmā a water-pot.
mantras.tr: Yama gave her a staff drawn from his own staff of death, and Varuṇa, lord of the waters, a noose; Prajāpati gave her a rosary, and Brahmā a water-pot.

comm.t: Yama gives a staff, Varuṇa a noose (his second gift, after the conch in 2.21), Prajāpati a rosary and Brahmā a water-pot. The last two are not weapons but the emblems of an ascetic and of the creator.
The noose (पाश) is Varuṇa’s ancient emblem, the bond with which he binds wrongdoers. In the battle the Goddess will use it to bind asuras and drag them along (2.57, पाशेन बद्ध्वा).

flags.uncertain: प्रजापतिश्चाक्षमालां ददौ ब्रह्मा कमण्डलुम्: with ददौ stated twice, the verse is taken as naming two givers, Prajāpati (as in 2.17, distinct from Brahmā) and Brahmā. It can also be read as one giver, ‘Brahmā the Prajāpati gave a rosary and a water-pot’, since Brahmā is called प्रजापति in 2.4. The reading itself is not in doubt.

samasa.sense: in every pore of her body

samasa.literal: that from which stain has gone

morph.note: Genitive of the recipient: with verbs of giving, epic and Purāṇic Sanskrit often uses the genitive where the classical language prefers the dative (contrast तस्यै in 2.20–22).
Accusative (= nominative) singular of the neuter n-stem चर्मन्: the final n is lost (चर्म).

mantras.anvaya: दिवाकरः समस्तरोमकूपेषु निजरश्मीन् (ददौ)। कालः च खड्गं निर्मलं चर्म च तस्याः दत्तवान्।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line has no verb of its own (ददौ from 2.23 is understood); the second is a full sentence with two objects.
mantras.lit: Into all the pores (of her skin) the Day-maker (set) his own rays; and Kāla gave her a sword and a spotless shield.
mantras.tr: The Sun filled every pore of her body with his own rays, and Time gave her a sword and a gleaming shield.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Filled’ is supplied for the missing verb of the first line.

comm.t: The Sun’s gift is not a weapon but his light, set into every pore of her skin: the Goddess shines from within. Kāla, Time, gives the sword and shield.
Kāla here is Time personified, a power that ends all things, and so a fitting giver of the sword. The sword and shield are among the weapons named in the dhyāna of the middle carita (असिं च चर्म).

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) calls the Goddess सर्वायुधधरा, ‘bearer of all weapons’ (name 530). In the Devī Māhātmya the same idea is told as a story: every weapon she holds was given to her by a god.

flags.uncertain: The first line has no finite verb; ददौ (or a verb of placing) is understood. Kāla is taken as Time personified, distinct from Yama (2.23), who is named separately.
